title: No. 60 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the Power of Congress to Regulate the Election of Members) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: We have seen that an uncontrollable power over elections to the federal government could not safely be committed to the State legislatures. Now let us see what the danger would be on the other side: trusting the Union itself with the ultimate right to regulate its own elections. No one claims that this right would ever be used to shut any State out of its share in the representation. The interest of all would, in this respect at least, be the security of all. But it is alleged that the right might be used to promote the election of some favorite class of men and exclude others. The means would be to confine the places of election to particular districts, making it impracticable for citizens at large to take part in the choice. Of all fanciful suppositions, this seems the most fanciful. On the one hand, no rational calculation of probabilities would lead us to imagine that the national councils could ever harbor the disposition so violent and extraordinary a course would imply. On the other hand, we may conclude with certainty that if so improper a spirit ever did gain entry, it would show itself in a quite different and far more decisive form.

We can fairly infer how improbable the attempt is from this one reflection: it could never be made without causing an immediate revolt of the great body of the people, led and directed by the State governments. In certain turbulent and factional seasons, it is not hard to imagine this characteristic right of liberty being violated against a particular class of citizens by a victorious and overbearing majority. But it is altogether inconceivable and incredible that so fundamental a privilege, in a country so situated and so enlightened, would be invaded to the injury of the great mass of the people by the deliberate policy of the government without bringing on a popular revolution.

Beyond this general reflection, there are more precise considerations that rule out any apprehension on the subject. The elements that will compose the national government are unlike one another, and the manner in which they will be brought into action in its various branches is more unlike still. This must form a powerful obstacle to any concert of views on a biased scheme of elections. The people of the different parts of the Union differ enough in the state of property, and in character, manners and habits, to produce a material difference of disposition among their representatives toward the different ranks and conditions of society. Close contact under one government will promote some gradual assimilation in certain of these respects. Even so, there are causes, physical as well as moral, that may in greater or lesser degree permanently nourish different inclinations on this point. But the circumstance likely to have the greatest influence will be the different ways of constituting the separate parts of the government. The House of Representatives is to be elected directly by the people, the Senate by the State legislatures, and the President by electors chosen for that purpose by the people. There would be little chance of a common interest to cement these different branches in a preference for any particular class of electors.

As for the Senate, no regulation of "time and manner" can affect the spirit that will direct the choice of its members. And "time and manner" is all that is proposed to be submitted to the national government with respect to that body. The collective view of the State legislatures can never be swayed by extraneous circumstances of that sort. This consideration alone ought to satisfy us that the feared discrimination would never be attempted. What inducement could the Senate have to agree to a preference in which it would not itself be included? And to what purpose would such a preference be established for one branch of the legislature if it could not be extended to the other? The make-up of the one would in that case counteract that of the other. We can never suppose that it would reach the appointments to the Senate unless we also suppose the voluntary cooperation of the State legislatures. If we make that supposition, it becomes immaterial where the power in question is placed, whether in their hands or in those of the Union.

But what is to be the object of this arbitrary bias in the national councils? Will it discriminate between the different departments of industry, or between the different kinds of property, or between the different degrees of property? Will it lean toward the landed interest, or the moneyed interest, or the mercantile interest, or the manufacturing interest? Or, in the fashionable language of the Constitution's adversaries, will it seek the elevation of "the wealthy and the well-born" while excluding and debasing all the rest of society?

Suppose this bias is to be exercised in favor of those engaged in some particular kind of industry or property. I presume it will readily be admitted that the competition for it would lie between landed men and merchants. And I do not hesitate to say that it is infinitely less likely that either of them would gain the upper hand in the national councils than that one or the other would dominate all the local councils. The inference is that we have much less to fear from the former than from the latter in conduct that tends to give an undue preference to either.

The individual States are devoted in varying degrees to agriculture and commerce. In most of them, if not all, agriculture is predominant. In a few, however, commerce nearly shares its empire, and in most it has a considerable share of influence. Whichever prevails will be carried into the national representation in proportion to its strength. But this representation will come from a greater variety of interests, in much more varied proportions, than any single State contains. For that very reason it will be much less apt to embrace either interest with decided partiality than the representation of any single State.

In a country made up chiefly of cultivators of land, where equal representation prevails, the landed interest must on the whole preponderate in the government. As long as that interest prevails in most of the State legislatures, it must keep a matching superiority in the national Senate, which will generally be a faithful copy of the majorities of those assemblies. It cannot be presumed, then, that sacrificing the landed class to the mercantile class will ever be a favorite object of this branch of the federal legislature. In applying a general observation, suggested by the situation of the country, specifically to the Senate, I am guided by this consideration: the credulous devotees of State power cannot, on their own principles, suspect that the State legislatures would be warped from their duty by any outside influence. But in reality the same situation must have the same effect, in the original composition at least of the federal House of Representatives. We should expect an improper bias toward the mercantile class as little from that quarter as from the other.

Perhaps, to give the objection some countenance in any case, someone will ask whether there is a danger of an opposite bias in the national government, disposing it to try to secure a monopoly of the federal administration for the landed class. Those who would be directly injured by such a bias are unlikely to find the supposition terrifying, so I will dispense with a labored answer to this question. It is enough to remark, first, that for the reasons given elsewhere, it is less likely that any decided partiality will prevail in the councils of the Union than in those of any of its members. Second, there would be no temptation to violate the Constitution in favor of the landed class, because that class would in the natural course of things enjoy as great a preponderance as it could want. Third, men used to examining the sources of public prosperity on a large scale must be too well convinced of the usefulness of commerce to be inclined to wound it as deeply as they would by excluding altogether from the management of public affairs those who would best understand its interest. In terms of revenue alone, the importance of commerce must effectively protect it from the enmity of a body that would be continually pressed on its behalf by the urgent calls of public necessity.

I am the more inclined to be brief on the probability of a preference based on discrimination between different kinds of industry and property because, as far as I understand the objectors, they have a different kind of discrimination in mind. They appear to have in view, as the objects of the preference with which they try to alarm us, those they describe as "the wealthy and the well-born." These, it seems, are to be raised to an odious pre-eminence over the rest of their fellow citizens. At one time, however, their elevation is to follow necessarily from the smallness of the representative body; at another, it is to be brought about by depriving the people at large of the chance to exercise their right to vote in choosing that body.

But on what principle is the discrimination of the places of election to be made, so as to serve the purpose of the intended preference? Are "the wealthy and the well-born," as they are called, confined to particular spots in the individual States? Have they, by some miraculous instinct or foresight, set aside a common place of residence in each of them? Are they found only in the towns or cities? Or are they, on the contrary, scattered over the countryside, wherever greed or chance has happened to place them or their predecessors? If the latter is the case (as every intelligent man knows it to be,(1)) is it not evident that confining the places of election to particular districts would defeat its own aim, besides being objectionable on every other account? The truth is that there is no way of securing the feared preference to the rich except by prescribing property qualifications for those who may elect or be elected. But that forms no part of the power to be given to the national government. Its authority would be expressly restricted to regulating the TIMES, the PLACES and the MANNER of elections. The qualifications of those who may choose or be chosen, as has been remarked on other occasions, are defined and fixed in the Constitution, and the legislature cannot alter them.

Still, let it be admitted for the sake of argument that the suggested expedient might succeed. Let it be equally taken for granted that the national rulers overcame every scruple that a sense of duty, or fear of the danger of the experiment, might awaken in them. Even so, I imagine no one will claim that they could ever hope to carry out such an enterprise without a military force large enough to subdue the resistance of the great body of the people. Different parts of these papers have discussed and demonstrated how improbable it is that a force equal to that object will exist. But to show the futility of the objection in the strongest light, let us concede for a moment that such a force might exist and that the national government actually possessed it. What will follow? Suppose they had a disposition to invade the essential rights of the community, and the means of gratifying it. Is it likely that persons moved by that disposition would amuse themselves with the ridiculous task of fabricating election laws to secure a preference for a favorite class of men? Would they not prefer a course better suited to their own immediate aggrandizement? Would they not rather boldly resolve to perpetuate themselves in office by one decisive act of usurpation than rely on precarious expedients? Such expedients, despite all the precautions that might accompany them, might end in the dismissal, disgrace and ruin of their authors. Would they not fear that citizens, as tenacious of their rights as they are aware of them, would flock from the remote ends of their States to the places of election to overthrow their tyrants and put in their place men disposed to avenge the violated majesty of the people?
1. Particularly in the Southern States and in this State.
